summary: Describes requirements for Securely Available Credentials protocols, which let users securely get their credentials, such as private keys, from different devices.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists what is needed to keep your keys in a safe place you can reach from anywhere.

questions: what is sacred securely available credentials
how to move private keys between devices
sacred credential server vs direct transfer
subtitle: What a protocol must do to let people move private keys and other credentials safely between their devices.

tldr.problem: People want to use the same credentials, such as private keys, from desktops, laptops, phones, pagers and PDAs, but in simple models credentials stay in one place.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for the SACRED framework and protocols: support for both credential-server and direct transfer, opaque credential formats, different transports and authentication schemes, a list of vulnerabilities to address, and numbered general, server and direct-transfer requirements.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only; the framework and the protocols are described in companion documents. Its direct-transfer list is explicitly provisional.

today: RFC 3157 is an Informational RFC; the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a requirements document, and the RFC points to companion documents for the framework and the protocols.

sections.title: Why Credentials Need to Move
sections.content:
Credentials are information used to establish an entity's identity or help it communicate securely, such as private keys, trusted roots, tickets or the private part of a Personal Security Environment. They support protocols like S/MIME, IPSec and TLS.

The RFC gives examples. Mimi wants to send signed e-mail from both her desktop and her laptop without recipients noticing a difference, so her private key must be on both. Will wants to read encrypted mail on a wireless phone or a two-way pager. A router's identity might also need to move to a bigger replacement router without editing every peer's configuration.

The private key must be transferred securely: not exposed to anyone else, sent to the proper device and not corrupted. The Working Group aims for protocols that work largely independent of the device and storage medium.
sections.plainLanguage: If your house key only works from one pocket, life is hard. You want the same key on all your jackets, without anyone copying it on the way.

sections.title: Framework Requirements: Server or Direct
sections.content:
There are two classes of solution. A credential server is active in the protocol: a user uploads credentials from one device and downloads them later to another. A direct transfer sends credentials device to device, and intermediate nodes only forward uninterpreted bits.

The server approach is conceptually clean, gives a place to store credentials for long periods and can enforce uniform policy. Its disadvantages are cost, the need to trust the server and a point of vulnerability, since someone with access can at least delete credentials. Direct transfer is more complex because of the many device types and formats, and each device may need to act as both client and server.

The framework requirements are:

  • F1: MUST support both server and direct solutions.
  • F2: they SHOULD use the same technology as far as possible.
  • F3: MUST allow different user authentication schemes.
  • F4: the credential type or format MUST be opaque to the protocol.
  • F5: MUST allow different transports.
sections.plainLanguage: You can leave your keys at a safe-deposit office and pick them up elsewhere, or hand them straight to your other device. The rules must allow both ways.

sections.title: General and Server Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements for all solutions include: transfer both to and from a device MUST be supported (G1); credentials MUST NOT be forced to appear in cleartext at any device other than the end user's (G2); transferred credentials SHOULD be authenticated, for example signed or MACed (G3); a range of cryptographic algorithms and various credential formats such as X.509, PGP and PKCS12 MUST be supported (G4, G5); one mandatory-to-support credential format and one mandatory user authentication scheme MUST be defined (G6, G7); and full internationalization via UTF-8 is REQUIRED (G9).

Server-based solutions add, among others:

  • S2: credentials MUST only be downloadable after user authentication, or in a format that needs authentication to decipher.
  • S3: authenticity MUST be ensurable during upload.
  • S7: the user SHOULD only need to enter a single secret.
  • S8: secrets MAY be shared across servers so that penetrating some does not expose a credential ("m-from-n").
  • S10, S11, S13: management operations, client-initiated password change and user self-enrollment MUST be supported.
  • S12: users SHOULD be able to list accesses and changes to their credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The main rule is that nobody in the middle may ever see your key in plain form, and you should only need to remember one secret to get it back.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities and Direct Transfer
sections.content:
Any protocol claiming to meet the requirements MUST explicitly say how, or whether, it protects against each listed vulnerability. The list of twelve (V1 to V12) includes passive dictionary attacks on captured packets, an attacker masquerading as the credential server or as a client, overwriting repository entries or someone else's uploaded credentials, copying a server's repository, forcing a password change to a known or weak password, man-in-the-middle attacks, a user typing a password instead of a name, and denial of service.

For direct transfer, the RFC says the full requirement set has not been worked out and the list is provisional; a further document, or a modification of this one, is needed before a direct-transfer protocol progresses. The two requirements so far are that the receiving device SHOULD be able to authenticate the sender (D1) and that it SHOULD be able to send an authenticated acknowledgment of receipt (D2).
sections.plainLanguage: The list names all the sneaky tricks a thief might try, and any design must say how it handles each one. The rules for passing keys hand to hand are still unfinished.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC admits mobile credentials will never be as secure as a pure hardware solution, because of potential attacks through the operating system of the end-user device. Downloaded-to platforms are usually not tamper-resistant, and storing even encrypted private keys on a server will be unacceptable in some environments. Replacing client software with a Trojan horse is always possible.

Implementations should audit security-relevant events (time, source, claimed identity, operation and result) without recording sensitive authentication data, and may mask the claimed identity in case a password is typed in the username field. Credential servers are major targets: a successful attack might expose or substitute users' credentials, for example by supplying a trusted root controlled by the attacker, and denial of service could force users to operate insecurely or not at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared key cabinet is a juicy target, so it needs a good lock, a visitor log that never writes down passwords, and protection from people who just want to block the door.
